paragraphs.text: Dorothy lived in the midst of the great Kansas prairies, with Uncle Henry, who was a farmer, and Aunt Em, who was the farmer's wife. Their house was small, for the lumber to build it had to be carried by wagon many miles. There were four walls, a floor and a roof, which made one room; and this room contained a rusty looking cookstove, a cupboard for the dishes, a table, three or four chairs, and the beds. Uncle Henry and Aunt Em had a big bed in one corner, and Dorothy a little bed in another corner. There was no garret at all, and no cellar—except a small hole dug in the ground, called a cyclone cellar, where the family could go in case one of those great whirlwinds arose, mighty enough to crush any building in its path. It was reached by a trap door in the middle of the floor, from which a ladder led down into the small, dark hole.

paragraphs.text: When Dorothy stood in the doorway and looked around, she could see nothing but the great gray prairie on every side. Not a tree nor a house broke the broad sweep of flat country that reached to the edge of the sky in all directions. The sun had baked the plowed land into a gray mass, with little cracks running through it. Even the grass was not green, for the sun had burned the tops of the long blades until they were the same gray color to be seen everywhere. Once the house had been painted, but the sun blistered the paint and the rains washed it away, and now the house was as dull and gray as everything else.

paragraphs.text: When Aunt Em came there to live she was a young, pretty wife. The sun and wind had changed her, too. They had taken the sparkle from her eyes and left them a sober gray; they had taken the red from her cheeks and lips, and they were gray also. She was thin and gaunt, and never smiled now. When Dorothy, who was an orphan, first came to her, Aunt Em had been so startled by the child's laughter that she would scream and press her hand upon her heart whenever Dorothy's merry voice reached her ears; and she still looked at the little girl with wonder that she could find anything to laugh at.

paragraphs.text: Hour after hour passed away, and slowly Dorothy got over her fright; but she felt quite lonely, and the wind shrieked so loudly all about her that she nearly became deaf. At first she had wondered if she would be dashed to pieces when the house fell again; but as the hours passed and nothing terrible happened, she stopped worrying and resolved to wait calmly and see what the future would bring. At last she crawled over the swaying floor to her bed, and lay down upon it; and Toto followed and lay down beside her.

Her face was covered with wrinkles, her hair was nearly white, and she walked rather stiffly.

paragraphs.text: "This at first seemed a great misfortune, for I knew a one-legged man could not do very well as a wood-chopper. So I went to a tinsmith and had him make me a new leg out of tin. The leg worked very well, once I was used to it. But my action angered the Wicked Witch of the East, for she had promised the old woman I should not marry the pretty Munchkin girl. When I began chopping again, my axe slipped and cut off my right leg. Again I went to the tinsmith, and again he made me a leg out of tin. After this the enchanted axe cut off my arms, one after the other; but, nothing daunted, I had them replaced with tin ones. The Wicked Witch then made the axe slip and cut off my head, and at first I thought that was the end of me. But the tinsmith happened to come along, and he made me a new head out of tin.

paragraphs.text: "I thought I had beaten the Wicked Witch then, and I worked harder than ever; but I little knew how cruel my enemy could be. She thought of a new way to kill my love for the beautiful Munchkin maiden, and made my axe slip again, so that it cut right through my body, splitting me into two halves. Once more the tinsmith came to my help and made me a body of tin, fastening my tin arms and legs and head to it, by means of joints, so that I could move around as well as ever. But, alas! I had now no heart, so that I lost all my love for the Munchkin girl, and did not care whether I married her or not. I suppose she is still living with the old woman, waiting for me to come after her.

paragraphs.text: "My body shone so brightly in the sun that I felt very proud of it and it did not matter now if my axe slipped, for it could not cut me. There was only one danger—that my joints would rust; but I kept an oil-can in my cottage and took care to oil myself whenever I needed it. However, there came a day when I forgot to do this, and, being caught in a rainstorm, before I thought of the danger my joints had rusted, and I was left to stand in the woods until you came to help me. It was a terrible thing to undergo, but during the year I stood there I had time to think that the greatest loss I had known was the loss of my heart. While I was in love I was the happiest man on earth; but no one can love who has not a heart, and so I am resolved to ask Oz to give me one. If he does, I will go back to the Munchkin maiden and marry her."

paragraphs.text: During the rest of that day there was no other adventure to mar the peace of their journey. Once, indeed, the Tin Woodman stepped upon a beetle that was crawling along the road, and killed the poor little thing. This made the Tin Woodman very unhappy, for he was always careful not to hurt any living creature; and as he walked along he wept several tears of sorrow and regret. These tears ran slowly down his face and over the hinges of his jaw, and there they rusted. When Dorothy presently asked him a question the Tin Woodman could not open his mouth, for his jaws were tightly rusted together. He became greatly frightened at this and made many motions to Dorothy to relieve him, but she could not understand. The Lion was also puzzled to know what was wrong. But the Scarecrow seized the oil-can from Dorothy's basket and oiled the Woodman's jaws, so that after a few moments he could talk as well as before.

And the Scarecrow found a tree full of nuts and filled Dorothy's basket with them, so that she would not be hungry for a long time. She thought this was very kind and thoughtful of the Scarecrow, but she laughed heartily at the awkward way in which the poor creature picked up the nuts. His padded hands were so clumsy and the nuts were so small that he dropped almost as many as he put in the basket. But the Scarecrow did not mind how long it took him to fill the basket, for it enabled him to keep away from the fire, as he feared a spark might get into his straw and burn him up. So he kept a good distance away from the flames, and only came near to cover Dorothy with dry leaves when she lay down to sleep. These kept her very snug and warm, and she slept soundly until morning.

paragraphs.text: This was to be an eventful day for the travelers. They had hardly been walking an hour when they saw before them a great ditch that crossed the road and divided the forest as far as they could see on either side. It was a very wide ditch, and when they crept up to the edge and looked into it they could see it was also very deep, and there were many big, jagged rocks at the bottom. The sides were so steep that none of them could climb down, and for a moment it seemed that their journey must end.

paragraphs.text: She left Dorothy alone and went back to the others. These she also led to rooms, and each one of them found himself lodged in a very pleasant part of the Palace. Of course this politeness was wasted on the Scarecrow; for when he found himself alone in his room he stood stupidly in one spot, just within the doorway, to wait till morning. It would not rest him to lie down, and he could not close his eyes; so he remained all night staring at a little spider which was weaving its web in a corner of the room, just as if it were not one of the most wonderful rooms in the world. The Tin Woodman lay down on his bed from force of habit, for he remembered when he was made of flesh; but not being able to sleep, he passed the night moving his joints up and down to make sure they kept in good working order. The Lion would have preferred a bed of dried leaves in the forest, and did not like being shut up in a room; but he had too much sense to let this worry him, so he sprang upon the bed and rolled himself up like a cat and purred himself asleep in a minute.

paragraphs.text: So the Tin Woodman followed him and came to the great Throne Room. He did not know whether he would find Oz a lovely Lady or a Head, but he hoped it would be the lovely Lady. "For," he said to himself, "if it is the head, I am sure I shall not be given a heart, since a head has no heart of its own and therefore cannot feel for me. But if it is the lovely Lady I shall beg hard for a heart, for all ladies are themselves said to be kindly hearted."

paragraphs.text: But when the Woodman entered the great Throne Room he saw neither the Head nor the Lady, for Oz had taken the shape of a most terrible Beast. It was nearly as big as an elephant, and the green throne seemed hardly strong enough to hold its weight. The Beast had a head like that of a rhinoceros, only there were five eyes in its face. There were five long arms growing out of its body, and it also had five long, slim legs. Thick, woolly hair covered every part of it, and a more dreadful-looking monster could not be imagined. It was fortunate the Tin Woodman had no heart at that moment, for it would have beat loud and fast from terror. But being only tin, the Woodman was not at all afraid, although he was much disappointed.

tts_chunks.speaker: narrator
tts_chunks.tts_text: The second time was when she had fought against the Great Oz himself, and driven him out of the land of the West. The Winged Monkeys had also helped her in doing this.

tts_chunks.tts_text: Only once more could she use this Golden Cap, for which reason she did not like to do so until all her other powers were exhausted.

paragraphs.text: Dorothy's life became very sad as she grew to understand that it would be harder than ever to get back to Kansas and Aunt Em again. Sometimes she would cry bitterly for hours, with Toto sitting at her feet and looking into her face, whining dismally to show how sorry he was for his little mistress. Toto did not really care whether he was in Kansas or the Land of Oz so long as Dorothy was with him; but he knew the little girl was unhappy, and that made him unhappy too.

paragraphs.text: Now the Wicked Witch had a great longing to have for her own the Silver Shoes which the girl always wore. Her bees and her crows and her wolves were lying in heaps and drying up, and she had used up all the power of the Golden Cap; but if she could only get hold of the Silver Shoes, they would give her more power than all the other things she had lost. She watched Dorothy carefully, to see if she ever took off her shoes, thinking she might steal them. But the child was so proud of her pretty shoes that she never took them off except at night and when she took her bath. The Witch was too much afraid of the dark to dare go in Dorothy's room at night to take the shoes, and her dread of water was greater than her fear of the dark, so she never came near when Dorothy was bathing. Indeed, the old Witch never touched water, nor ever let water touch her in any way.

So that when Dorothy walked across the floor she stumbled over the bar, not being able to see it, and fell at full length. She was not much hurt, but in her fall one of the Silver Shoes came off; and before she could reach it, the Witch had snatched it away and put it on her own skinny foot.

paragraphs.text: You will remember there was no road—not even a pathway—between the castle of the Wicked Witch and the Emerald City. When the four travelers went in search of the Witch she had seen them coming, and so sent the Winged Monkeys to bring them to her. It was much harder to find their way back through the big fields of buttercups and yellow daisies than it was being carried. They knew, of course, they must go straight east, toward the rising sun; and they started off in the right way. But at noon, when the sun was over their heads, they did not know which was east and which was west, and that was the reason they were lost in the great fields. They kept on walking, however, and at night the moon came out and shone brightly. So they lay down among the sweet smelling yellow flowers and slept soundly until morning—all but the Scarecrow and the Tin Woodman.

paragraphs.text: "Once," began the leader, "we were a free people, living happily in the great forest, flying from tree to tree, eating nuts and fruit, and doing just as we pleased without calling anybody master. paragraphs.text: "There lived here then, away at the North, a beautiful princess, who was also a powerful sorceress. All her magic was used to help the people, and she was never known to hurt anyone who was good. Her name was Gayelette, and she lived in a handsome palace built from great blocks of ruby. Everyone loved her, but her greatest sorrow was that she could find no one to love in return, since all the men were much too stupid and ugly to mate with one so beautiful and wise. At last, however, she found a boy who was handsome and manly and wise beyond his years. Gayelette made up her mind that when he grew to be a man she would make him her husband, so she took him to her ruby palace and used all her magic powers to make him as strong and good and lovely as any woman could wish. When he grew to manhood, Quelala, as he was called, was said to be the best and wisest man in all the land, while his manly beauty was so great that Gayelette loved him dearly, and hastened to make everything ready for the wedding.

paragraphs.text: "My grandfather was at that time the King of the Winged Monkeys which lived in the forest near Gayelette's palace, and the old fellow loved a joke better than a good dinner. One day, just before the wedding, my grandfather was flying out with his band when he saw Quelala walking beside the river. He was dressed in a rich costume of pink silk and purple velvet, and my grandfather thought he would see what he could do. At his word the band flew down and seized Quelala, carried him in their arms until they were over the middle of the river, and then dropped him into the water.

paragraphs.text: "The princess was angry, and she knew, of course, who did it. She had all the Winged Monkeys brought before her, and she said at first that their wings should be tied and they should be treated as they had treated Quelala, and dropped in the river. But my grandfather pleaded hard, for he knew the Monkeys would drown in the river with their wings tied, and Quelala said a kind word for them also; so that Gayelette finally spared them, on condition that the Winged Monkeys should ever after do three times the bidding of the owner of the Golden Cap. This Cap had been made for a wedding present to Quelala, and it is said to have cost the princess half her kingdom. Of course my grandfather and all the other Monkeys at once agreed to the condition, and that is how it happens that we are three times the slaves of the owner of the Golden Cap, whosoever he may be."

So the Scarecrow at last asked the green girl to take another message to Oz, saying if he did not let them in to see him at once they would call the Winged Monkeys to help them, and find out whether he kept his promises or not. When the Wizard was given this message he was so frightened that he sent word for them to come to the Throne Room at four minutes after nine o'clock the next morning. There were four of them in this country, and they ruled the people who live in the North and South and East and West. Fortunately, the Witches of the North and South were good, and I knew they would do me no harm; but the Witches of the East and West were terribly wicked, and had they not thought I was more powerful than they themselves, they would surely have destroyed me. As it was, I lived in deadly fear of them for many years; so you can imagine how pleased I was when I heard your house had fallen on the Wicked Witch of the East. When you came to me, I was willing to promise anything if you would only do away with the other Witch; but, now that you have melted her, I am ashamed to say that I cannot keep my promises."

paragraphs.text: The great spider was lying asleep when the Lion found him, and it looked so ugly that its foe turned up his nose in disgust. Its legs were quite as long as the tiger had said, and its body covered with coarse black hair. It had a great mouth, with a row of sharp teeth a foot long; but its head was joined to the pudgy body by a neck as slender as a wasp's waist. This gave the Lion a hint of the best way to attack the creature, and as he knew it was easier to fight it asleep than awake, he gave a great spring and landed directly upon the monster's back. Then, with one blow of his heavy paw, all armed with sharp claws, he knocked the spider's head from its body. Jumping down, he watched it until the long legs stopped wiggling, when he knew it was quite dead.

characters.name: Dorothy
characters.persona: Dorothy is a polite, innocent, plainspoken child who speaks in short, earnest questions and mild exclamations like "Oh, dear!" and "Oh, gracious!". She is quick to laugh and to be startled, yet she settles into calm, patient curiosity, and she answers elders with hesitant courtesy ("You are very kind, but there must be some mistake"). She takes things literally and honestly, asking direct questions of strangers without suspicion or pretension.

characters.name: Witch of the North
characters.persona: She is gentle, courteous and calm, greeting a stranger with a low bow and a sweet, formal voice ("You are welcome, most noble Sorceress") yet laughing easily and taking grim matters in stride ("There is nothing to be done"). She speaks plainly and patiently, explaining things step by step in tidy, slightly old-fashioned sentences, with confident assertions ("I know this is true... and cannot be mistaken"), and addresses the child kindly as "my dear" while asking simple questions of her own. She lowers her voice to a whisper when naming something awesome, and handles distress with solemn, quietly whimsical composure.

characters.name: Wicked Witch of the West
aliases: the Wicked Witch of the West
characters.persona: She is harsh, imperious and cruel, speaking in a shrill, cackling, sneering voice that snaps out orders and threats. She is sharp-tempered and spiteful, mocking anyone weaker than herself and never raising her voice in kindness. Her sentences are short, bullying and full of menace.

characters.name: Oz
characters.persona: He speaks in a grand, commanding, booming manner, formal and weighty, addressing visitors as supplicants in short, imperious declarations. He is aloof and impatient with idle talk, and expects to be obeyed without argument.

characters.name: Scarecrow
characters.persona: Courteous and old-fashioned in his diction, the Scarecrow says "Certainly," "I shall be greatly obliged," and "Thank you very much," and speaks in full, carefully reasoned sentences. He is good-humored and gently self-deprecating, cheerfully accepting his shortcomings and laughing at his own mishaps, yet he turns wistful and a bit sad when he talks about what he lacks. He is friendly and curious, asking direct questions, eagerly offering help, and lowering his voice to share a confidence with a phrase like "I'll tell you a secret."

characters.name: Tin Woodman
characters.persona: The Tin Woodman speaks in a courteous, formal, slightly old-fashioned way, with grave sincerity and effusive gratitude, thanking people again and again. He is earnest and sentimental, prone to pausing to think deeply before making a request, and fond of weighing matters in measured, reasoned statements such as "True" or "after all." When he tells his tale he turns eloquent and wistful, with exclamations like "alas," and he addresses companions plainly and politely, offering practical advice and firm opinions about happiness and the heart.

characters.name: Cowardly Lion
characters.persona: He blusters in with a roar but quickly turns sheepish, speaking in a mild, candid, politely rueful voice that owns up to his faults without excuse. He is melancholy and self-pitying, given to sad sighs, hanging his head, and phrases like "I know it" and "how can I help it?", yet he is curious and thoughtful, asking simple questions and answering with an earnest, slightly formal courtesy ("if you don't mind, I'll go with you"). He is agreeable and eager to please, deferring to others and treating them as companions rather than rivals.

characters.name: Glinda
characters.persona: She is gracious, warm and queenly, speaking in gentle, courteous, unhurried sentences and addressing visitors as 'my dear' or 'my child'. Kind and serene, she explains things patiently and smiles often, with a quiet poise that puts people at ease.

summaries.text: Dorothy lives on the gray Kansas prairie with Uncle Henry, a farmer, and Aunt Em, his wife, in a small one-room house with a cyclone cellar reached by a trap door. Dorothy, an orphan, is cheered by her little black dog Toto, while the adults have grown gray and joyless from hard work and weather. One day Uncle Henry sees a cyclone approaching from the north and south. He goes to the sheds to tend the animals, and Aunt Em hurries down into the cellar, leaving Dorothy to follow with Toto. The wind lifts the house high into the air and carries it a great distance. Dorothy rescues Toto after he falls through the open trap door, then lies down on her bed and falls asleep as the house is tossed about.

Dorothy, an orphan, lives on the gray Kansas prairie with Uncle Henry and Aunt Em, whose hard lives have left them joyless, and her little black dog Toto is her comfort. A cyclone lifts their small house and carries it far away, and Dorothy falls asleep on her bed as it is tossed through the air. She wakes to find the house has landed gently in a beautiful land, crushing the Wicked Witch of the East. Dorothy takes the dead witch's silver shoes. Munchkins thank her for freeing them, and the Witch of the North tells her that Oz the Great Wizard rules the Emerald City, that the deserts and neighboring countries block other routes, and that she must follow the yellow brick road there. The witch gives her a protective kiss and vanishes. Dorothy then sets out alone with Toto, wearing the silver shoes, after a stay in a Munchkin house. At Boq's house a feast and dance honor her, and Boq warns her of the long, dangerous road. Along the way she rescues a talking Scarecrow from a pole in a cornfield. He says he has no brains and asks to come to Oz for some, so he joins her, carrying her basket, while Toto distrusts him. He confesses that he fears only a lighted match.

The current chapter so far: Dorothy and the Scarecrow travel along the yellow brick road, which grows rough and broken, and the Scarecrow repeatedly tumbles into the gaps. At noon by a brook Dorothy eats bread while the Scarecrow, who cannot eat because his mouth is painted and his straw would spill out, asks about Kansas. She describes its grayness and the cyclone that brought her to Oz, and the Scarecrow says he cannot understand why anyone would prefer Kansas. He then recounts how the farmer made him, painting his ears, eyes, nose and mouth, and how he was left on a stake in a cornfield where an old crow told him that only brains matter. He hopes the Great Oz will give him brains at the Emerald City. Toward evening they enter a dark forest, and the Scarecrow guides Dorothy to a log cottage where she sleeps while he stands waiting until morning.

The current chapter so far: After Dorothy wakes and the party breakfasts at a spring, they hear groans and find a tin man frozen beside a half-chopped tree, his joints rusted. Dorothy and the Scarecrow oil his neck, arms and legs, freeing him, and he thanks them, explaining he has groaned for over a year unheard. Dorothy explains they are going to the Emerald City to see Oz, she to return to Kansas and the Scarecrow for brains. The Tin Woodman asks to join them, hoping Oz can give him a heart. Dorothy gives him a heart-hopeful reply, and he takes his axe and joins the party on the yellow brick road. He chops a passage through overgrown branches, and when the Scarecrow falls into a hole, the Woodman says he once had brains and a heart and would rather have a heart. The Scarecrow asks why.

He tells his story: the enchanted axe, cut by the Wicked Witch of the East, took first his legs, arms, head and body, each replaced by tin by a tinsmith, leaving him heartless and no longer in love with his Munchkin sweetheart. The Scarecrow wants brains and the Woodman wants a heart, and they disagree over which matters more. Dorothy worries that the bread is nearly gone, since she must eat and the others need not.

The Scarecrow and Woodman wonder whether he has a heart or brains, and each companion states a wish to ask Oz for something: brains, a heart, a return to Kansas, or courage. The Lion, saying his life is unbearable without courage, decides to join them.

The current chapter so far: The travelers camp in the forest, where the Scarecrow gathers nuts for Dorothy and lays dry leaves over her to keep her warm, while the Lion hunts alone and the Tin Woodman refuses to let him kill a deer. The next day they reach a deep, wide ditch with jagged rocks at the bottom. The Lion carries the Scarecrow, then Dorothy with Toto, then the Tin Woodman across it in three leaps. In the gloomy forest the Lion warns them of the Kalidahs, bear-bodied beasts with tiger heads. A second gulf blocks the road, so the Woodman chops down a tree to bridge it. Two Kalidahs charge; the Lion roars to frighten them, and the Scarecrow has the Woodman cut the far end of the tree so that both beasts fall into the gulf and are killed on the rocks. The forest thins, and by afternoon they reach a swift river with a yellow-brick road and fruit-laden trees beyond it. The Woodman begins building a raft, and Dorothy eats ripe fruit the Scarecrow found for her.

Oz asks about the silver shoes and the mark on her forehead, then tells her she must kill the Wicked Witch of the West before he will send her back to Kansas. She weeps and goes back to her room. The Scarecrow, the Tin Woodman and the Lion each see Oz in a different form, a lovely Lady, a terrible Beast and a Ball of Fire, and each is given the same condition: the Witch must be destroyed first. The friends resolve to set out for the land.

Dorothy, an orphan, lives on the gray Kansas prairie with Uncle Henry and Aunt Em, until a cyclone lifts their house and carries it to the magical Land of Oz, where it lands on the Wicked Witch of the East. Freed Munchkins hail her, the Witch of the North kisses her and sends her along the yellow brick road to the Emerald City, and she takes the dead witch's silver shoes. Along the road she rescues a Scarecrow who wants brains, then a rusted Tin Woodman who wants a heart, and then a Cowardly Lion who wants courage. In a dark forest they survive a Lion's attack, and the Woodman and Scarecrow kill two Kalidahs by felling a tree into a gulf. A swift river carries the group off course, and a poppy meadow puts Dorothy and the Lion to sleep. Field mice, led by their Queen, haul the Lion out of the flowers. At the Emerald City, a green Guardian fits them with spectacles locked on by a golden key. Inside the green city, Dorothy meets the Wizard Oz as a great Head, who demands that she kill the Wicked Witch of the West before he will send her home to Kansas. She weeps in her room. The Scarecrow, Tin Woodman and Lion each see Oz in a different form and receive the same condition. The friends resolve to set out for the Witch's land.

The current chapter so far: Dorothy and her companions leave the Emerald City, guided by the Guardian of the Gates toward the West, where the Wicked Witch lives. Dorothy's silk dress and Toto's ribbon have turned white. Tired from the hot afternoon sun with no shade, they sleep while the Scarecrow and Woodman keep watch. The Wicked Witch, who has one far-seeing eye, sees them and sends a pack of forty wolves, which the Woodman kills with his axe. She then sends forty wild crows, which the Scarecrow kills by twisting their necks. Next come black bees; Dorothy hides under the Scarecrow's straw and the bees break their stings on the Woodman's tin. The Witch then sends twelve Winkie slaves with spears, who flee when the Lion roars. The Witch recalls that the Golden Cap has three uses, two already spent, and takes it from her cupboard, putting it on her head and standing on her left foot to begin speaking the charm.

The Monkeys smash the Tin Woodman on rocks, strip the Scarecrow of his straw, and tie up the Lion in the Witch's yard. In anger, Dorothy throws a bucket of water over the Witch, who begins melting away and asks whether Dorothy did not know water would destroy her.

The Witch sends wolves, crows and bees against them; the Woodman, the Scarecrow and the straw blanket defeat the first two attacks and the bees, and the Winkies are chased off by the Lion. The Witch then uses the third and last call of the Golden Cap, and the Winged Monkeys tear the Woodman and Scarecrow apart and tie up the Lion in her yard. They spare Dorothy because of the Good Witch's kiss on her forehead, and the Witch makes Dorothy her servant. The Witch tries to harness the Lion, starves him, and schemes for the Silver Shoes. She trips Dorothy with an invisible iron bar and takes one shoe. When Dorothy throws a bucket of water over her, the Witch melts away. Dorothy recovers the shoe and runs to free the Lion.

Dorothy, an orphan, lives on the gray Kansas prairie with Uncle Henry and Aunt Em, with only her little dog Toto to cheer her. A cyclone lifts their house and carries it to the magical land of Oz, where it lands on the Wicked Witch of the East. Dorothy takes the dead witch's silver shoes, and the Witch of the North tells her to follow the yellow brick road to the Emerald City and the Great Oz. On the road she frees a Scarecrow who wants brains, then a Tin Woodman who wants a heart, then a Cowardly Lion who wants courage. Together they survive the forest, the Kalidahs, and the river, and a poppy field that nearly kills the Lion until the Queen of the Field Mice and her thousands of mice rescue him. At the Emerald City, the Wizard appears to each companion in a different form and sets one condition: the Wicked Witch of the West must be destroyed first. The friends set out for her castle in the Winkie country. There the Witch sends wolves, crows and bees, and her Winged Monkeys tear the Scarecrow and Woodman apart and capture the Lion. The Witch enslaves Dorothy, starves the Lion, and takes one of the silver shoes after tripping Dorothy. Dorothy throws water on the Witch, who melts away, and she recovers the shoe and runs to free the Lion.

The current chapter so far: Once the Wicked Witch has been melted by water, Dorothy frees the Cowardly Lion from his prison and the two go to the castle, where she tells the yellow Winkies they are no longer slaves, and they celebrate with feasting and dancing. Dorothy and the Lion lead Winkies to fetch the battered Tin Woodman, who is carried back to the Yellow Castle, where tinsmiths spend three days and four nights mending him. Dorothy wipes his tears with her apron to keep his joints from rusting. The Woodman then offers to cut down a tall tree that holds the Scarecrow's clothes; a Winkie goldsmith has meanwhile given his axe a gold handle. Once the tree falls, the Scarecrow is restored, and the group resolves to return to Oz for their wishes: a heart, brains, courage, and Dorothy's return to Kansas. The Winkies bid them farewell with gifts, and Dorothy takes the Golden Cap from the Witch's cupboard and wears it. The travellers then set out for the Emerald City.

At the Emerald City, the Wizard appears as a great Head and demands that they destroy the Wicked Witch of the West before he grants their wishes. Captured in the Witch's castle, Dorothy is made her servant, and the Winged Monkeys tear apart the Scarecrow and the Woodman while the Lion is tied up. Dorothy escapes when she throws water on the Witch, who melts away. The Winkies are freed, and the friends repair the Woodman and restore the Scarecrow. They now resolve to return to the Emerald City to claim their wishes, and Dorothy wears the Golden Cap from the Witch's cupboard as they set out.

The current chapter so far: Dorothy, the Scarecrow, the Tin Woodman, the Cowardly Lion and Toto are lost in the fields of scarlet and yellow flowers, unable to tell east from west, and grow discouraged. Dorothy calls on the Queen of the Mice, who explains that the Golden Cap carries a charm that summons the Winged Monkeys. Dorothy reads the charm inside the Cap and speaks it while standing on different feet. The Monkeys, led by their King, carry the travelers through the air toward the Emerald City, with the Scarecrow and Woodman uneasy at first but then content. On the flight, the King tells Dorothy how the Monkeys came to obey the Cap's owner: Gayelette, a sorceress princess of the North, wanted to marry Quelala, whom the Monkeys dropped into a river to spoil his silks. Gayelette spared them on condition that they obey the Cap's owner three times over. The King adds that the Wicked Witch of the West later used the Cap to enslave the Winkies, and that Dorothy now holds the Cap and its three wishes.

Dorothy speaks the charm and the Monkeys, led by their King, carry the companions to the gates of the Emerald City. The Cap was a wedding gift to Quelala, Gayelette's intended husband, after the Monkeys had dropped him into a river. The travelers arrive safely, and the Lion remarks on their good luck in having the Cap.

Along the way she gathers companions: the Scarecrow, who wants brains; the Tin Woodman, who wants a heart; and the Cowardly Lion, who wants courage. Together they overcome the Kalidahs, cross a river, and escape the sleep-inducing poppy field with the help of the Queen of the Field Mice. At the Emerald City, Oz tells them they must first destroy the Wicked Witch of the West. The companions travel to her castle, where her Winged Monkeys attack them and capture the Lion, the Scarecrow and the Woodman. Dorothy, who is spared, melts the Witch with a bucket of water, frees the Lion, and the Winkies are freed. The Woodman and the Scarecrow are repaired, and the group sets out again for the Emerald City, guided by the Golden Cap, whose Winged Monkeys carry them to the city gates after the Monkey King explains the Cap's history.

The current chapter so far: The four travelers return to the Emerald City and are admitted by the Guardian of the Gates, who is astonished to hear that Dorothy melted the Wicked Witch of the West. A crowd follows them to the Palace, where the green-whiskered soldier and the green girl receive them. Oz delays for several days, so the Scarecrow sends a threat to summon the Winged Monkeys, and Oz, frightened, orders them to the Throne Room the next morning. There, an invisible Voice claims to be Oz the Great and Terrible and asks what they want. Dorothy, the Scarecrow, the Tin Woodman and the Lion demand their promised rewards: Dorothy's return to Kansas, brains, a heart, and courage. The Voice asks whether the Witch is really destroyed and asks for another day to think, but the travelers refuse to wait. When the Lion roars, Toto knocks over a screen, revealing a small, bald, wrinkled old man who begs not to be struck and confesses he has been making believe. Each traveler had imagined Oz differently, and the Wizard admits he is not the.

The Scarecrow returns to his friends proud and feeling wise, though pins stick out of his head. Next the Tin Woodman asks for a heart; Oz cuts a square hole in his left breast, places a silk heart stuffed with sawdust inside, and solders the tin patch back. Finally the Cowardly Lion asks for courage and drinks a liquid from a green bottle, after which he reports feeling full of courage. Each companion leaves the Throne Room happy with the gift received, and the chapter stops with the Lion rejoining the group.

In the Winkie country the Witch captures them and enslaves Dorothy, but Dorothy throws water on her and melts her. The Winkies are freed, and the Woodman and Scarecrow are repaired. The Golden Cap summons the Winged Monkeys, who carry the companions back to the Emerald City. There the Wizard is revealed as a humbug, a ventriloquist from Omaha who arrived by balloon..

The current chapter so far: After three sad days in which Dorothy heard nothing from Oz, the Wizard sends for her and proposes crossing the desert by balloon, since he came to the country by balloon and she by cyclone. He admits he is a humbug and wants to leave the Emerald City, so he will go with her. Dorothy helps sew green silk strips into a large bag, which Oz coats with glue. The Tin Woodman builds a fire and the Wizard heats the bag until it rises, tethered to a clothes basket. Dorothy runs back for Toto, and when the ropes snap the balloon rises without her. Oz calls goodbye from the basket and drifts away. The people grieve and say the Scarecrow now rules the city in his place.
